p: Eleazar is not the brothers' father: "father" is a title of honor for the old priest and teacher.
b: The speaker calls Eleazar "our father" (7:1, 5, 9), the way Jews spoke of honored elders and teachers. He is not the father of the seven: the brothers call him "our old teacher" (9:6), and their own father appears only in the mother's last speech (18:9-19). R. B. Townshend (1913) notes that Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on the martyrs, has Eleazar call the youths his sons, which Townshend takes in a spiritual sense, since in 4 Maccabees Eleazar was plainly not their father. The Orthodox Church in America's life of the saints for 1 August calls him "their teacher Eleazar", beside "their mother Solomonia".

p: Reason is a ship's pilot holding the tiller in a storm of passions and tortures, until it reaches harbor.
b: Three verses carry one picture: the pilot (kybernētēs), the steering (pēdalioucheō), the tillers (oiakes), the great waves (trikymiai, literally "third waves", the biggest ones) and at last the harbor. The passions are the sea; the tyrant's threats and the tortures are the storm. The speaker will use the harbor again for the seven brothers, whose reason is like towers on harbor walls that break the waves (13:6-7). James uses a ship to make a smaller point about the tongue: "a tiny rudder steers them wherever the helmsman's urge decides" (James 3:4).

t: The soul as a city under siege
p: The picture changes from sea to war: Eleazar's soul is a besieged city that will not open its gates.
b: The "many kinds of siege engines" (mēchanēmata) are the torture instruments, seen as the battering machines of an army. The city held out "through the reason that stood as a shield over godliness". The speaker returns to the image for the brothers' "seven-towered" reason (13:7). Proverbs uses the same idea the other way round: a person who cannot rule his spirit is a city with its walls broken down (Proverbs 25:28).

a: you did not defile your holy teeth
p: Eleazar's teeth are called "holy", most likely because he is a priest; pork would have defiled them.
b: 4 Maccabees makes Eleazar a priest (5:4), where 2 Maccabees calls him a scribe (2 Maccabees 6:18). The verse does not say why his teeth are holy. A likely reason, inferred from the law rather than stated in the book, is that a priest ate the holy portions of the offerings once he was clean (Leviticus 22:6-7), so his mouth and stomach could be spoken of as holy vessels. The food was pork, which the law forbids: "It is unclean for you" (Leviticus 11:7). Daniel likewise "set his heart on not defiling himself with the king's rich food" (Daniel 1:8). The Greek word for the eating of defiling food is miarophagia, which Swete's Alexandrinus spells mierophagia (Sinaiticus has miaro-, as Swete's notes show).

p: The speaker calls a Jewish priest a philosopher: for him the law of Moses is the true philosophy.
b: Philosophos theiou biou, "philosopher of a divine life". In Greek cities a philosopher was someone who lived by reason and taught others to. The speaker claims that title for a man who kept the food laws, and later the brothers "argued philosophy back" at the tyrant (8:15). Eleazar had said the king mocked "our philosophy" (5:22). Townshend (1913) sums up the book's aim as showing "how Greek philosophy can help an orthodox Jew to keep the Law".

p: The Greek pathos means both "passion" and "suffering", and the speaker plays on both.
b: The noun pathos (plural pathē) is the book's key word: reason rules "the passions". But the same word also means what a person suffers. Here Eleazar shields the law "in sufferings (pathesin) that go to the point of death". The pun runs through the martyr stories: the men who master their passions do it in the middle of their sufferings, and they are "sovereign over their pains" (8:28). English cannot keep one word for both, so the Plain English Translation uses "passions" for the inner drives and "sufferings" here.

a: Our father Aaron took up the censer
p: The scene is Numbers 16, where Aaron ran with incense into the crowd and stopped a plague.
b: After Korah's revolt, Moses told Aaron to take fire and incense and "make atonement for them" (Numbers 16:46). Aaron "ran into the middle of the assembly". "He stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was held back" (Numbers 16:47-48). Numbers names no angel. The Wisdom of Solomon tells the same scene and says that "With a word he brought the punisher under control" and "To these the destroyer gave way" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:22, 25). 4 Maccabees goes a step further and calls the destroyer "the angel who was burning them", like "the angel who was destroying among the people" in David's time (2 Samuel 24:16). The first hand of Sinaiticus lacks the words "who was burning" (see the variant). Townshend (1913) counts this verse, with a question mark, among the places where the book shows belief in angels.
r: Numbers 16:35; Numbers 16:41-50; Wisdom of Solomon 18:20-25; 2 Samuel 24:16; 1 Chronicles 21:15

p: The Greek coins a family name, Aarōnidēs, "son of Aaron", to present Eleazar as a true priest.
b: Greek poets named heroes by their ancestors ("Atreides", son of Atreus). The speaker gives Eleazar such a name, ho Aarōnidēs, from Aaron. It fits the claim that he was "a priest by family" (5:4), and it may also recall the first Eleazar, Aaron's own son and successor (Exodus 6:25; Numbers 20:25-28). The point of 7:11-12 is that the new Eleazar, like Aaron, stood firm in fire for the sake of the people.

p: Isaac is the model of a willing victim: the book later says he endured being offered by his father.
b: In Genesis Abraham "bound his son Isaac and put him on the altar, on top of the wood" (Genesis 22:9), and Isaac says almost nothing. 4 Maccabees reads the story as Isaac's own choice: the brothers remind each other at whose father's hand Isaac "endured" to be slaughtered for godliness (13:12), and the mother recalls Abraham hurrying to offer him (16:20). Eleazar, an old man, gains a young man's strength by thinking as Isaac did. The "many-headed rack" is a torture that keeps striking like the many-headed Hydra of Greek myth; Townshend (1913) renders it "the hydra-headed torture".

p: A seal closed and confirmed a document; death set the seal on Eleazar's life and made it complete.
b: The verb is eteleiōsen, "perfected, brought to completion". A life lived by the law is finished and certified by a faithful death, the way a seal finishes a letter or a will. Revelation gives a similar promise to a persecuted church: "Stay faithful all the way to death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10).

t: Why not everyone rules the passions
p: The speaker answers an objection: if reason rules the passions, why do so many people give in to them?
b: His answer (7:18-23) is that only reason fully given to godliness can rule; a weak reason loses (7:20). This echoes a Greek teaching. The Stoics held that virtue is the only good and gave the name "Sage" to the ideal human being, the only one who truly has knowledge (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Stoicism"). 4 Maccabees agrees that such mastery belongs to few, but its "wise man" is the one who trusts God and keeps the law (7:21-22). Paul draws a darker line between the mind that agrees with the law and the flesh that does not obey it (Romans 7:22-25).

t: "They live to God" and Jesus' answer to the Sadducees
p: The same idea, that the patriarchs live to God, is Jesus' argument in Luke 20:38. Here it is not about resurrection.
b: Jesus answered the Sadducees from the bush: God calls himself "the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob". "He is not God of dead people but of living ones, for to him all are alive" (Luke 20:37-38; compare Mark 12:26-27). Luke's last clause (pantes gar autō zōsin) is very close to 4 Maccabees' zōsin tō theō. Townshend (1913) calls Mark 12:26 the closest parallel, and reports that I. Abrahams, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, thought passages of this kind might be Christian additions; Townshend saw no reason why a Jewish writer could not say it. The book says it again at 16:25. Paul writes, "When we live, we live for the Lord. When we die, we die for the Lord" (Romans 14:8). In Sinaiticus the sentence reads "just as our patriarchs ... did not (die) either" (oude for gar), as Swete's notes show; the sense is the same.

t: Compared with the Bible: life with God, but no resurrection here
p: 4 Maccabees hopes for the soul's life with God at death; 2 Maccabees and the New Testament hope for the body's rising.
b: Agrees. The faithful dead belong to God and are alive to him (Luke 20:38; Romans 14:8; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1). Differs. When Jesus says it, he is answering the question whether "the dead are raised" (Luke 20:37). 2 Maccabees has the second brother say, "But the King of the world will raise us, who died for his laws, to live again forever" (2 Maccabees 7:9), and Daniel 12:2 promises a waking from the dust. 4 Maccabees retells the same martyrs without a word about their bodies rising. Townshend (1913) put it plainly: "Apparently there is no resurrection of the body" in the book; the righteous are received into bliss at death. Churches that read 4 Maccabees in their Bibles read it beside 2 Maccabees and the Creed, which confess the resurrection of the dead.

p: Kanōn is a measuring rod, a rule to live by; Paul uses it for a rule of life, and the church later for its list of books.
b: A kanōn was a straight rod used for measuring. Greek moralists used it for a standard of conduct. Paul blesses "all who will walk by this rule" (Galatians 6:16), and later Christians called their list of accepted books "the canon". Here the rule is philosophy, lived "in a godly way" and joined to trust in God: the speaker will not let philosophy stand apart from faith.

a: the brave lord over the passions
p: A Stoic-sounding saying, but the book does not ask, as the Stoics did, that the passions be rooted out.
b: "Only the wise man" is the shape of the Stoics' famous sayings about the Sage. The verse names three of the four virtues the book listed at the start (1:2-4, 18): wisdom or good sense, self-restraint, and courage. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that the Stoics "famously argue that the virtuous agent feels no passions". 4 Maccabees means something else by mastery. Townshend (1913) says the author "upholds the Stoic virtues, though not the Stoic" apatheia (freedom from passion): the passions remain, but reason trained by the law rules them (3:2-5). Sinaiticus leaves out "self-restrained" (see the variant).

p: The speaker calls them "young men", "lads" and "boys"; 2 Maccabees gives no ages at all.
b: The words vary: neaniai, "young men" (8:5; 8:27), meirakia, "lads" (8:14; 11:24), and here meirakiskoi, "young boys", which is used of the sixth (11:13). The youngest is a "boy" (pais, 12:6, 9). Calling them boys sharpens the argument: if even boys can rule the passions by godly reason, no grown hearer has an excuse (7:24; 8:1). 2 Maccabees calls the youngest "the young man" (2 Maccabees 7:25, 30).

a: very much in the grip of passion
p: The man who wants to master the martyrs cannot master himself: he acts "very passionately".
b: The adverb peripathōs, "under strong emotion", is built on pathos, "passion". The irony is deliberate. The king who claims to rule the Hebrews is himself ruled by anger (8:9; 9:10), while the boys he tortures are "sovereign over their pains" (8:28). In 2 Maccabees, too, "The king flew into a rage" (2 Maccabees 7:3).

a: they were to be let go after eating
p: Brother after brother is offered his freedom for one bite. Hebrews 11:35 speaks of martyrs who would not take release.
b: The offer comes again and again: "let go" (8:2), "rid of the tortures" (9:16), "eat and be let go" (11:13). Hebrews says of the faithful who suffered: "Others were tortured on the rack and would not take the release they were offered, so that they could win a better resurrection" (Hebrews 11:35). The verb there, etympanisthēsan, comes from the same root as the noun tympanon, Eleazar's torture frame in 2 Maccabees (2 Maccabees 6:19, 28); the lexicon LSJ lists Hebrews 11:35 under the verb tympanizō. Hebrews also hopes for resurrection, which 2 Maccabees 7 preaches and 4 Maccabees does not. So Hebrews stands closer to 2 Maccabees than to this book, though both tell of the same martyrs.

a: seven brothers were brought in, together with their aged mother
t: Compared with 2 Maccabees: the family arrives
p: 2 Maccabees says only that seven brothers were arrested with their mother; 4 Maccabees adds their looks and the king's smile.
b: 2 Maccabees begins, "It also happened that seven brothers were arrested along with their mother" (2 Maccabees 7:1), and goes straight to the whips. 4 Maccabees slows down: the boys are handsome and modest, they stand around their mother like a chorus, the king smiles and makes a long speech of friendship (8:5-11). Neither book names the brothers or the mother. Later tradition did: the Orthodox Church in America's life of the saints for 1 August names them Abim, Antonius, Gurias, Eleazar, Eusebonus, Alimus and Marcellus, and their mother Solomonia. The Talmud tells of "the woman and her seven sons" brought before an emperor (Bavli Gittin 57b).

p: To the king, dying for the law is madness. The word comes back in the guards' mouths (10:13).
b: The Greek doubles the word: mēnēnai tēn autēn ... manian, "to rage the same madness". In 2 Maccabees Eleazar's guards turned against him "because they took what he had said to be madness" (2 Maccabees 6:29). The guards repeat the charge to the fourth brother (10:13), and the king calls the brothers' stand "folly" (12:4). Townshend (1913) notes that some called Antiochus Epiphanes, "the Brilliant", and some Epimanes, "the Madman": in this book the madness belongs to the king.

a: the ancestral rule of your way of life as a people
p: The king asks them to give up their "citizenship": the law that made the Jews a people with their own rights.
b: Ton patrion hymōn tēs politeias thesmon, "the ancestral ordinance of your citizenship". In Greek cities a politeia was a people's civic life and constitution. For Jews the law of Moses was that constitution, and kings had granted them the right to live by it. 2 Maccabees tells how the high priest Jason "moved his own people over to the Greek stamp" and "did away with the lawful ways of life" (2 Maccabees 4:10-11). The king's offer, "Take part in Greek life" (8:8), asks the brothers to finish what Jason began.
orig: τὸν πάτριον ὑμῶν τῆς πολιτείας θεσμόν

t: A new way of life, or a new menu?
p: The verb means to change one's daily way of living, and diaita also means diet. Both fit a test about food.
b: Metadiaitēthentes is built on diaita, "way of living, regimen", the word behind English "diet". The king means "change your whole way of life", and the test he sets is a meal. At the end the speaker uses the same root when he says the king could not force the people of Jerusalem "to be cut off from their fathers' nation" (ekdiaitēthēnai, 18:5). The Plain English Translation says "diet" so the reader hears the link to the food law.

p: Several of these Greek words are rare, and the shape of most of the machines is not known.
b: The list: wheels; joint-wrenchers (arthrembola: LSJ, the standard Greek lexicon, gives "instrument for setting limbs" in Galen and "instruments of torture" here; Townshend "joint-dislocators"); racks; trochantēres (LSJ: "an instrument of torture" here; elsewhere the knob at the head of the thigh bone; "bone-crushers" is Townshend's guess); catapults; kettles; griddles; thumbscrews (daktylēthrai, from daktylos, "finger": LSJ "thumb-screw" here, as Townshend); iron hands; wedges; and ta zōpyra tou pyros. LSJ gives zōpyron as a live coal for kindling and, in Ephorus, a pair of bellows; the Plain English Translation takes the second sense. Townshend has "branding irons"; Erasmus's Latin, which he quotes, has succensoria, a thin iron tool for stirring up the flame. A katapeltēs was a war machine for hurling missiles; here it is a frame a victim was bound to (9:26; 11:9-10, 26). The kettles and griddles are those of 2 Maccabees 7:3 ("griddles and kettles"). The copies spell several of the words differently (see the variant).

p: Greeks pictured Justice (Dikē) as a goddess; the king assumes the Jews worship such a power.
b: In Greek religion Dikē, Justice, was a goddess who saw wrongs and punished them. The islanders of Malta said of Paul, "Justice won't let him go on living" (Acts 28:4). The king talks as if the Jews served such a goddess, who could be talked round. In the brothers' mouths the same word becomes "divine Justice" (8:22; 9:9; 12:12) and "heavenly Justice" (9:15; 11:3), God's justice that the king cannot bribe. The Plain English Translation writes Justice with a capital J where the Greek treats it as a person.

a: what words would they have used?
t: The speech that was never made
p: The speaker invents what cowards would have said, a device of Greek rhetoric, then tells us no one said it.
b: Ancient speakers often put words in the mouths of their characters to show what was at stake. Here the speaker goes further and writes a speech the brothers did not make (8:17-26), every excuse a frightened person might use: pity for our youth and our mother, God will forgive us, the law does not want us dead. Then he says, "But the young men about to be tortured said none of these things" (8:27). Townshend (1913) writes of all the martyrs' speeches in the book: "Dramatic inventions they doubtless are, like most other speeches that have come down to us from antiquity", while warning against calling them impossible.

a: Divine Justice too will forgive us
t: May a Jew break the law to save his life?
p: The cowards' argument is not foolish: later Jewish law allows most commandments to be broken to save a life, but not under persecution.
b: The Talmud records a ruling taken in an upper room at Lod: a person told to break a commandment or be killed may break it, except for three, idol worship, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed (Bavli Sanhedrin 74a). The Talmud bases it on Leviticus 18:5, "If a human being does them, he will live by them": the commandments were given for living. But it adds, in the name of Rabbi Yohanan, that "in a time of religious persecution", when the rulers try to force Jews to violate their religion, "even if they issued a decree about a minor mitzva, one must be killed and not transgress". Antiochus's decree is just such a time, so the brothers' choice agrees with this later rule. 4 Maccabees itself argues the point through Eleazar: to break the law in small things and in great is the same (5:20).

p: Autokratōr, "sovereign", is the word in the book's later title, On the Supremacy of Reason.
b: The brothers are autokratores tōn algēdonōn, "sovereigns over pains". The thesis of the book is that godly reason is sovereign over the passions. Townshend (1913) says the oldest title is simply "Maccabees" (the fourth book), as in Alexandrinus, Sinaiticus and Venetus; but the work, once attributed to Josephus, also appears among his writings under a title taken from its subject, peri autokratoros logismou, which Townshend renders "On the Supremacy of Reason", and Eusebius and Jerome cite it under that title. In the Roman world autokratōr was also the Greek for "emperor": the boys are the real emperors, not the king.

p: All seven answer together, as one person, before any of them is tortured.
b: In 2 Maccabees one brother speaks for all (2 Maccabees 7:2). Here all seven speak "with one voice, as though from one soul", which prepares for the long praise of their brotherly love (13:19-27). Acts says of the first believers, "The great company of believers had one heart and one soul" (Acts 4:32).

a: We are ready to die sooner than break the commandments of our fathers
t: Compared with 2 Maccabees: the first answer
p: Almost the very words of 2 Maccabees 7:2, with "commandments" for "laws", and spoken by all seven, not one.
b: 2 Maccabees: "We are ready to die sooner than break the laws of our fathers" (2 Maccabees 7:2). The Greek of the two books is nearly the same: hetoimoi gar esmen apothnēskein ē parabainein, with tas patrious hēmōn entolas, "our ancestral commandments", in place of tous patrious nomous, "the ancestral laws". This is one of the clearest signs that the writer knew the story in the form 2 Maccabees gives it, or in a source both books used; Townshend (1913) leaves open whether the additions come from the writer or from Jason of Cyrene, the lost work that 2 Maccabees summarizes.

p: The Greek says "our souls", psychas, which can mean "lives"; the brothers will soon say their souls cannot be touched.
b: Tas hēmōn psychas ei thanatōseis, literally "if you put our souls to death". Psychē is "soul", but it is also the everyday word for a person's life, and that is the sense here. The book's own teaching is that the soul cannot be reached by torture (10:4) and goes free at death (9:25). So the Plain English Translation says "lives" here and keeps "soul" where the Greek means the inner self.

p: Athla were prizes in the games: the brothers see their torture as a contest with a crown at the end.
b: The noun athla belongs to the stadium. The image grows through the chapters: a "training ground" (11:20), "champions" or contestants (12:15), and finally the great picture of the martyrs as athletes and the tyrant as their opponent (17:11-16). Townshend (1913) notes how freely the writer uses the Greek games. Paul uses the games too: "They do it to receive a crown that fades. We do it for one that never fades" (1 Corinthians 9:25), and Hebrews calls the church to run "the race that lies ahead of us" (Hebrews 12:1).

p: A pun: the king wanted them to commit mierophagia, "defiled eating"; he commits mierophonia, "defiled killing".
b: The noun mierophonia, "foul murder", is a near rhyme with mierophagia, "the eating of defiling food". The brothers turn the charge round: the king thought they would be defiled by a meal, but the one who is defiled is the man who kills them. The third brother uses a similar word, miaiphonia, "bloodshed" (10:11), and the king is called "most foul" (mierōtatos) again and again (9:15, 32; 10:10).

t: Compared with the Bible: eternal fire for the persecutor
p: The brothers promise the king fire without end. The 66 books also speak of unending fire; they also teach praying for persecutors.
b: Agrees. Isaiah ends with the rebels whose "fire will not be put out" (Isaiah 66:24), and Jesus speaks of Gehenna "where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:48). Revelation says of those who worship the beast, "The smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever" (Revelation 14:11). The brothers say the same of their tyrant (10:11; 12:12, 19). Differs in spirit. Townshend (1913) noted: "There is here no trace of the spirit of the Crucified", who prayed, "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34). Stephen prayed, "Lord, do not count this sin against them!" (Acts 7:60).
r: 10:11; 12:12; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:43-48; Revelation 14:10-11; Luke 23:34; Acts 7:60; Matthew 5:44

t: Compared with 2 Maccabees: who suffered what
p: 4 Maccabees keeps the seven deaths but changes the tortures and their order. A brother-by-brother comparison.
b: 2 Maccabees has all seven "tortured with whips and cords" (2 Maccabees 7:1). Then: the first loses tongue, scalp, hands and feet and is fried (2 Maccabees 7:4-5); the second is scalped (2 Maccabees 7:7); the third gives his tongue and hands (2 Maccabees 7:10-11); the fourth suffers "the same torture" (2 Maccabees 7:13); no tortures are named for the fifth and sixth (2 Maccabees 7:15, 18); the youngest is treated worst (2 Maccabees 7:39). In 4 Maccabees: the first is whipped, racked on the wheel and burned (9:11-25); the second is skinned with iron hands (9:26-28), the one close match; the third has his joints wrenched and is scalped (10:5-8); the fourth loses his tongue (10:17); the fifth is bent on the catapult (11:9-11); the sixth is burned with spits and thrown into a kettle (11:17-19; 12:1); the seventh throws himself on the griddles (12:20). The torture list of 8:13 is spread across the seven.

a: not abusing me like this because I murdered anyone
p: In 2 Maccabees two brothers say "we suffer for our own sins". In 4 Maccabees no brother confesses sin.
b: In 2 Maccabees the sixth brother says, "We suffer this because of ourselves; we sinned against our own God" (2 Maccabees 7:18), and the youngest, "We suffer for our own sins" (2 Maccabees 7:32): the persecution is God's discipline of the nation. 4 Maccabees drops these lines. Its brothers insist on their innocence: the first is tortured not as a murderer or an ungodly man "but because I defend the divine law"; the youngest says the king killed "the champions of virtue for no reason" (12:15). The nation's sin appears later, when the speaker says their deaths were "a life in exchange" for it (17:21-22). Both views have roots in the 66 books: the nation punished for its sins (Deuteronomy 28:15; Daniel 9:4-11), and the righteous who suffer without cause (Psalm 44:17-22; Job 1:8).

p: The verb is unclear: Swete's axai most likely means "to break"; Sinaiticus has angxai, "to choke".
b: Swete prints axai, which can come from agnymi, "to break, shatter". Townshend (1913) renders it "to lead captive", taking it from agō, "to lead". Sinaiticus reads angxai, "to strangle", the verb used in all the copies at 10:7 ("they could not choke him"). Each gives the same idea: no torture can overpower the reason of a man devoted to God.

p: The book's favorite name for the martyrs is "Abraham's children": here an adjective, "Abrahamic young man".
b: Ho Abramiaios neanias, "the Abrahamic young man". The first hand of Sinaiticus wrote "Abraham's son" instead, as Swete's notes show. The speaker ends by calling his hearers children of Abraham's seed (18:1). The New Testament uses the same kind of title: Jesus calls Zacchaeus "a son of Abraham" (Luke 19:9) and a crippled woman "a daughter of Abraham" (Luke 13:16), and Paul says that "the ones who are from faith, these are the sons of Abraham" (Galatians 3:7).

a: as though the fire were changing him into incorruption
p: The verbs recall Paul: the body "refashioned" and the perishable putting on "what cannot decay". Paul means resurrection.
b: The participle metaschēmatizomenos, "being changed in form", is the verb of Philippians 3:21: "He will refashion (metaschēmatisei) the body we have in our low state". Aphtharsia, "incorruption", is Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 15: "This thing that decays has to put on what cannot decay" (1 Corinthians 15:53). The Wisdom of Solomon says, "For God created the human being for incorruption" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:23). The difference is important: Paul speaks of the body raised and changed at Christ's coming; 4 Maccabees speaks "as though", a picture of a soul made deathless while the body burns.

p: The first brother makes himself a pattern for the others, as Eleazar meant his death to be one for the young.
b: Eleazar in 2 Maccabees says that "to the young I will leave behind a fine pattern" (2 Maccabees 6:28). Here the oldest brother asks his brothers to copy him, and later they cheer each other on to copy the three young men of Daniel (13:9). Paul uses the same verb: "Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ" (1 Corinthians 11:1).

p: The language turns military: deserting the line, swearing off an oath, fighting a campaign.
b: Leipotakteō is a soldier's word, "to leave one's place in the battle line"; exomnymi, "to swear off", fits a soldier's oath; and they are to "campaign a campaign" (strateian strateusasthe) for godliness. The brothers fight with no weapons but endurance. Paul writes to Timothy, "Suffer hard things along with me, as Christ Jesus' good soldier" (2 Timothy 2:3).

p: The word means a wretch who deserves vengeance, and also the avenging spirit that pursues a crime.
b: LSJ, the standard Greek lexicon, gives alastōr two senses: an "avenging spirit or deity", frequent in Greek tragedy, and, in the passive sense, "he who does deeds which merit vengeance, wretch". Here the king is "this accursed tyrant", the rendering the Plain English Translation also uses at 18:22. At 11:23 the sixth brother uses the first sense: by dying he will bring "a great avenger" down on the king. The second brother of 2 Maccabees calls the king by the same word, which the site's 2 Maccabees renders "You fiend" (2 Maccabees 7:9).

p: The Greek says he "broke off his soul", a Greek way of saying a person died.
b: Aperrēxen tēn psychēn, "he broke off his soul". LSJ, the standard Greek lexicon, lists this verb with "spirit", "life" or "soul" as its object as a way of saying "snap the thread of life, die". The Plain English Translation says "life" here, as it does where psychē means a person's life. The phrase fits the book's belief that the soul is the self, kept safe from the torturer (10:4) and gathered at death to the patriarchs (13:17). Townshend (1913) traces this Alexandrian belief in the immortal soul without bodily resurrection, which he calls "usually attributed to their having come under the influence of the philosophy of Plato and the neo-Pythagoreans".

p: The torturers are "leopards" and the king a "savage beast" (12:13). Daniel pictured the persecuting kingdoms as beasts.
b: The speaker calls the guards hoi pardalioi thēres, "the leopard-like wild beasts", and the youngest calls the king thēriōdestate, "most beastly" (12:13). Daniel saw the empires as beasts, one "another beast, like a leopard" (Daniel 7:6). The book does not say it is alluding to Daniel; the shared picture is that cruelty to the faithful makes rulers less than human.

a: How sweet is every kind of death
p: The second brother calls every death sweet if it is for God; the apostles rejoiced to suffer for the Name.
b: The speaker's thesis is at work: pain is overcome by a greater pleasure, "the pleasures that virtue brings" (9:31). The apostles left the council "glad at heart, because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name" (Acts 5:41), and Paul could write, "For me, living is Christ and dying is gain" (Philippians 1:21). The book's opening said the two roots of the passions are pleasure and pain (1:20); here a higher pleasure masters the worst pain.

p: The brothers' father is never present in the story; the mother speaks of him only at the end (18:9-19).
b: The third brother rests his claim on family: one father, one mother, one upbringing. The father is not in the story; the mother's last speech remembers him as a man who taught his sons the Scriptures and has since died (18:9-19). The "teachings" (dogmata) on which they were raised are the law's teachings, the same word used of the decrees of the Jewish faith in Greek-speaking Judaism.

a: You will not touch my soul
p: The torturers can reach only the body. Jesus says the same to his disciples, and Wisdom says no torment touches the souls of the righteous.
b: Jesus told the Twelve, "do not fear the people who kill the body but have no power to kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28); the brothers will say something like it at 13:14-15. The Wisdom of Solomon uses the same verb "touch" (haptomai): "no torment will touch them at all" (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1). A Roman historian noticed the belief among Jews: "they think the souls of those killed in battle or by execution are eternal" (Histories of Tacitus 5:5). Sinaiticus lacks this verse (see the variant).
r: 13:14-15; 9:7; Matthew 10:28; Luke 12:4-5; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1; Histories of Tacitus 5:5

p: The Greek is unclear: the victim's fingertips were torn off with the skin, or the torturers used their fingertips.
b: Perisyrantes to derma syn akrais tais tōn daktylōn koryphais apeskythizon: "stripping off the skin with the very tips of the fingers, they scalped him". Townshend (1913) takes the fingertips as the victim's: "stripped off his skin, taking the points of the fingers with it". Others take the phrase as the torturers' fingertips, as if they peeled him by hand. The scalping "the way the Scythians do" repeats 2 Maccabees 7:4 (see the note there on Scythian scalping).
orig: σὺν ἄκραις ταῖς τῶν δακτύλων κορυφαῖς

a: the training and the virtue that come from God
p: Paideia is education and discipline. The book calls the law "the training" by which divine and human things are learned (1:17).
b: Dia paideian kai aretēn theou: "because of the training and the virtue that come from God". The genitive "of God" may go with both words: the training God gives and the virtue God gives. At the start the speaker said that the law's paideia teaches divine things with reverence and human things for our good (1:16-17). The brothers die for their schooling.

p: The king is Antiochus IV of the Seleucid kingdom, who banned Jewish practice in 167 BC.
b: The speaker named him Antiochus Epiphanes when the king came to the throne (4:15). Here he names him again, with three insults in a row: "bloodthirsty" (literally "blood-eating", haimoboros), "murderous", "all-defiled". Antiochus IV ruled the Seleucid kingdom of Syria and outlawed the Jewish law, as 1 and 2 Maccabees tell (1 Maccabees 1:41-64; 2 Maccabees 6:1-11). Townshend (1913) notes his nicknames, Epiphanes, "the Brilliant", and Epimanes, "the Madman". "Blood-eating" fits the book's theme: the man who forces forbidden food on others feeds on their blood.

p: God hears prayer that makes no sound, as he heard Hannah, whose voice no one could hear.
b: Hannah prayed so quietly that "Her lips were trembling, but no one could hear her voice" (1 Samuel 1:13), yet God answered her. Paul says that the Spirit pleads for us "with groanings that words cannot say" (Romans 8:26). The fourth brother's answer to the knife is that prayer does not need a tongue.

a: Look, my tongue is hanging out
t: Compared with 2 Maccabees: the offered tongue
p: In 2 Maccabees the third brother put out his tongue at once; here it is the fourth, and he adds a saying about reason.
b: 2 Maccabees: "Asked for his tongue, he stuck it out at once, and he stretched out his hands without fear" (2 Maccabees 7:10). 4 Maccabees moves the scene to the fourth brother and gives it a philosopher's turn: cutting out his tongue will not "cut out our reason's tongue". The verb glōssotomeō, "to cut out the tongue", is used again by the youngest (12:13).

a: a tongue that sang hymns to God
p: The tongue the king cuts out had sung God's praise: the king is silencing worship.
b: The psalmists often promise to praise God with the tongue: "Then my tongue will tell of your righteousness" (Psalm 35:28). The fourth brother's last words turn that worship into a charge against the king: God "will soon come after" the man who cuts out a praising tongue.

p: The fifth brother is not dragged in: he volunteers. Was it right to seek martyrdom?
b: He comes "on my own" (11:3), and the youngest will throw himself onto the griddles (12:20). Christian preachers praised this eagerness: Townshend (1913) observes that Gregory of Nazianzus, in his oration on the Maccabees, "makes the youths boldly demand the torture for themselves, their only fear being lest any should be denied the crown of martyrdom". Jesus, on the other hand, told his disciples, "When they hunt you down in this town, escape to the next" (Matthew 10:23). The difference matters: the brothers are already arrested and facing the order to eat; none of them goes looking for the king. On the youngest brother's leap, see the note on 12:20.

p: Pagan writers called the Jews haters of humankind. Here a Jewish martyr says it of the persecuting king.
b: Misanthrōpe, "hater of human beings". Greek and Roman writers often accused the Jews of hating other peoples because they kept apart in food and worship. The Roman historian Tacitus wrote that among themselves their loyalty is stubborn, "but toward everyone else they feel hostile hatred" (Histories of Tacitus 5:5). In this book the charge is turned round: the man who tortures boys for keeping their food laws is the real enemy of humankind, and the youngest will remind him that they share his nature (12:13).

p: The fifth brother joins creation and law: the God who made all things gave the law that teaches virtue.
b: The mother in 2 Maccabees appeals to "the Creator of the world" (2 Maccabees 7:23). Here the son calls God ton pantōn ktistēn, "the Creator of all", and calls his law enaretos, "full of virtue". The book's claim is that the law and the order of nature come from the same Maker, so keeping the law cannot be against nature, as Antiochus had argued (5:8-9).

p: Gymnasia is athletic training. The brothers' gymnasium is the torture ground, not the one Jason built in Jerusalem.
b: Eis gymnasian ponōn, "to a training of toils". The word recalls the Greek gymnasium, where young men trained naked for the games. 2 Maccabees tells how the high priest Jason "was glad to found a gymnasium at the very foot of the citadel" (2 Maccabees 4:12), and 4 Maccabees says the same (4:20). Townshend (1913) remarks that the writer, though he condemns Jason's gymnasium, freely compares the martyrs to athletes. Here the true Jewish young men train by enduring pain for godliness.

p: Epistēmē is knowledge or understanding; godly understanding is a near synonym for the book's "godly reason".
b: The sixth brother says hē eusebēs epistēmē, "godly understanding", where the book usually says "godly reason". The speaker had defined wisdom as knowledge of divine and human things and of their causes (1:16), and said it is learned through the law (1:17). For him, knowing God's law rightly and ruling the passions belong together.

t: The blood of the martyrs cries out
p: The sixth brother says his death will add to the vengeance against the king. Abel's blood and the souls under the altar cry out too.
b: God told Cain, "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). In Revelation the souls of those slain for God's word cry out, "How long, Master, holy and true?" and ask God to "avenge our blood on them" (Revelation 6:10). The fifth brother had said the same: each death adds to what the king will "owe heavenly Justice" (11:3). On the word "avenger" (alastōr) see the note on 9:24.

a: the guards who stand over us serve not a tyrant but the divine law
p: The tyrant's own guards end up serving God's law: the more they torture, the more they prove the law's power.
b: The doryphoroi, "spear-bearers", were a king's bodyguard. The sixth brother claims them for the other side: by bringing out the brothers' steadfastness, they are standing guard for the divine law. It is a last reversal in a chapter of reversals: fire is cold, catapults painless, force powerless (11:26), and the boys have "brought down" the tyranny (11:24).

a: The tyrant felt sorry for him
p: The Talmud's version also has the emperor pity the youngest and offer him an easy way out.
b: In 2 Maccabees the king pleads with the youngest and promises him wealth (2 Maccabees 7:24). In the Talmud's story of "the woman and her seven sons", each son refuses to worship the idol with a verse from the Torah. When the youngest refuses, "the emperor pitied him" and offered to throw down his seal, asking the boy only to bend and pick it up "so that people will say that he has accepted the king's authority". The boy refused (Bavli Gittin 57b; see the note on 2 Maccabees 7:41). The two versions share the king's pity and his search for a face-saving way out; 4 Maccabees sets the scene beside the griddles.

p: "Friend" was a title at the Seleucid court, a rank with honors and offices.
b: The king promises the boy the rank of philos, "Friend", and a share in running the kingdom. 2 Maccabees has the same offer: "he would have him as a Friend and hand him important tasks" (2 Maccabees 7:24). The king's officers promised Mattathias that he would be "counted among the Friends of the King" (1 Maccabees 2:18).

p: The mother speaks so that the king cannot understand. "Hebrew" in Greek can mean Hebrew or Aramaic.
b: Tē Hebraidi phōnē, "in the Hebrew voice". 2 Maccabees says the mother spoke "in their fathers' tongue" (2 Maccabees 7:21, 27). Greek writers of the time used "Hebrew" both for Hebrew and for the Aramaic that Jews spoke: John calls Gabbatha, an Aramaic name, the place's name "in Hebrew" (John 19:13), and Paul addressed the crowd "in Hebrew" (Acts 21:40). "As we will tell a little later": her speech comes at 16:16-23, which is also said to be given in the Hebrew tongue (16:15). Townshend (1913) notes that Erasmus, in his Latin version, moved her speech here instead of keeping it back as the author did.

a: those who train themselves in godliness
p: Askētai were people in training, athletes and disciplined philosophers; the word gave English "ascetic".
b: The youngest calls his brothers tous tēs eusebeias askētas, "the trainees of godliness". An askētēs was anyone who practiced a discipline, above all an athlete. The image matches the "training ground" of 11:20. Paul tells Timothy, "train yourself toward godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7), using the gymnasium's verb. Christian monks were later called ascetics from this word.

p: The youngest appeals to shared humanity: the king is torturing people "of like feelings" with himself.
b: Tous homoiopatheis, "those who suffer and feel as you do". Paul and Barnabas told the crowd at Lystra, "We are human too, with feelings just like yours" (Acts 14:15), and James says "Elijah was a man who felt what we feel" (James 5:17), both with the same Greek word. "Made from the same elements" uses the philosophers' word for the building blocks of the world (stoicheia). Solomon says in the Wisdom of Solomon, "I too am a mortal, the equal of everyone" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:1).

t: Compared with the Bible: a prayer for the nation
p: The youngest, like the youngest in 2 Maccabees, ends with a prayer that God be merciful to his people.
b: 2 Maccabees: "I call, as they did, on God to be gracious soon to the nation" (2 Maccabees 7:37), with the same Greek adjective, hileōs. The first brother wished the same of providence (9:24), and Eleazar asked God to be merciful to his nation (6:28). The speaker will say that God answered: the martyrs became "a life in exchange" for the nation's sin (17:21-22). Whether the sufferings of faithful people can help atone for others, or only Christ's death atones, is the question of the "Where Christians differ" card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38. Agrees with the intercession of Moses, who offered to be blotted out for the people (Exodus 32:32), and with the servant who "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12).

a: both in this present life and when you are dead
p: The book claims both: Antiochus was punished on earth and is punished after death (18:5).
b: At the close the speaker says it came true: the tyrant Antiochus has been punished on earth, and after his death he is still punished (18:5). 2 Maccabees tells his death in Persia, struck with pain in his bowels: "Worms came boiling up out of the impious man's body" (2 Maccabees 9:9). 1 Maccabees has him die of grief after defeat (1 Maccabees 6:8-16).

a: he threw himself down onto the griddles
p: The youngest is not thrown: he throws himself. Jews and Christians have praised and puzzled over such deaths.
b: In 2 Maccabees the king killed the youngest "more cruelly than with the rest" (2 Maccabees 7:39). Here the boy, once untied, runs to the griddles and throws himself down on them, and the mother later throws herself into the fire so that no guard would touch her body (17:1, the same verb). Jewish readers. The Talmud praises four hundred captive children who asked, "If we commit suicide and drown in the sea, will we come to eternal life in the World-to-Come?", and then leapt into the sea rather than be used for prostitution, applying to them, as to the woman and her seven sons, the verse "For Your sake we are killed all the day long" (Bavli Gittin 57b). Christian readers. John Chrysostom, as Townshend (1913) reports, preached that the youngest leapt into the braziers "as they had been fountains of cool waters, reckoning them a divine font and baptism". Augustine held that no canonical book permits suicide (City of God 1.20), but would not judge the holy women honored as martyrs who drowned themselves to escape "those who menaced them with outrage", suggesting they may have been "prompted by divine wisdom", as Samson was (City of God 1.26). The chapter page discusses the question.
